result: The FM-based inducible ER release system successfully retains GluA1 and NL1 in the ER prior to DDS addition and enables synchronous release and surface delivery following DDS treatment. Both cargoes show robust surface delivery within 2-8 hours and localize appropriately to dendrites and spines.
evaluation: Claims C25-C35 demonstrate effective ER retention, inducible release, and surface delivery of both GluA1 and NL1 using the FM system. The data show appropriate ER localization before release (C25, C27), GA accumulation after release (C26, C28), and time-dependent surface delivery (C29-C34) with proper dendritic/spine localization (C35). The system is validated in both COS7 cells and neurons with consistent results.

result: GluA1 released from dendritic ER remains spatially segregated from somatically-released GluA1, with only 12.9% of dendritically photoconverted signal reaching the soma and 93.3% of somatically photoconverted signal remaining in the somatic GA. This demonstrates that post-ER trafficking organelles are determined by the cellular location of ER exit.
evaluation: Claims C36-C43 and C102-C103 provide strong evidence for spatial segregation using photoconversion experiments. The quantitative data (C38, C39) show striking compartmentalization with minimal crosstalk between dendritic and somatic trafficking networks. The length constant of 11.6 µm (C42) further supports local trafficking. The experimental design appropriately controls for ER continuity and protein mobility.

result: Following ER exit at 20°C, GluA1 accumulates in dendritic puncta that colocalize with ERGIC53 but not with classical Golgi markers (GM130, TGN38). Colocalization with ERGIC53 peaks at 50-60 minutes post-release, indicating ERGIC is the first post-ER compartment for dendritic cargo.
evaluation: Claims C44-C49 demonstrate that dendritic GluA1 puncta are ERGIC structures, not Golgi outposts. The temperature block at 20°C (C44, C45, C114) appropriately stalls trafficking for identification. The lack of GM130/TGN38 colocalization (C46) combined with strong ERGIC53 colocalization (C48) and time-dependent dynamics (C49) provide convincing evidence. The widespread ERGIC distribution (C47) is consistent with prior literature.

result: Some transport from somatic GA to dendritic regions (especially proximal dendrites) can occur, as demonstrated by photobleaching recovery experiments.
evaluation: Claim C51 is supported by photobleaching recovery data showing a proximal-to-distal gradient of recovered signal (Figure 4—figure supplement 4). However, this represents a minor trafficking route compared to the local dendritic pathway, as evidenced by the strong spatial segregation shown in other experiments. The claim appropriately acknowledges this is primarily relevant for proximal regions.

result: ERGIC and recycling endosome (RE) membranes show frequent spatial juxtaposition throughout dendrites that is statistically significant and not due to chance. STED microscopy reveals ERGIC structures ranging from 60-400 nm in diameter that are often immediately adjacent to TfR-positive REs.
evaluation: Claims C52-C55 provide strong evidence for ERGIC-RE spatial proximity using both confocal and super-resolution STED microscopy. The randomization control (C53) demonstrates statistical significance beyond chance colocalization. STED imaging (C54, C55) provides nanoscale resolution confirming close apposition. This spatial relationship supports the hypothesis of functional coupling between these organelles.

result: Following ER release, GluA1 progressively accumulates in recycling endosomes marked by TfR and Rab11, with co-trafficking increasing from ~32-37% at 60 minutes to ~53-60% at 150 minutes. This RE-mediated forward trafficking applies to both integral membrane proteins (GluA1, NL1) and soluble secretory cargo (4xFM-mCh).
evaluation: Claims C56-C65 and C104 demonstrate robust RE involvement in forward trafficking using multiple complementary approaches: live imaging (C56), photobleaching assays (C57-C61), thrombin controls (C62), and soluble cargo (C63-C64). The time-dependent increase in co-trafficking and the near-absence of GluA1 in REs before release (C57) strongly support anterograde rather than recycling trafficking. The generality across different cargo types (C64, C65) strengthens the conclusion.

result: GluA1 accumulates in a subset of spine-resident recycling endosomes following ER release, with 20.6% of RE-positive spines containing GluA1 at 150 minutes. Spines with REs show higher surface GluA1 than neighboring RE-negative spines, and nearly all (97%) spines containing spine apparatus also contain REs.
evaluation: Claims C66-C71 and C111 demonstrate spine-specific delivery through REs. The quantification of GluA1 in spine REs (C69) with thrombin controls eliminates recycling artifacts. The differential surface delivery between RE-positive and RE-negative spines (C70) supports functional significance. The strong correlation between spine apparatus and REs (C71) suggests potential local ER-to-RE trafficking. The predominance of dendritic insertion events (C66) is consistent with local delivery.

result: Dominant-negative Rab11(S25N) significantly impairs GluA1 surface delivery at early timepoints (2 and 4 hours), while Rab8(T22N) impairs delivery only at later timepoints (4 hours). Rab5(S34N) has no effect, indicating REs but not early endosomes are critical for forward trafficking.
evaluation: Claims C72-C75 and C92 provide genetic evidence for RE involvement using dominant-negative constructs. The differential timing of Rab11 vs. Rab8 effects (C72-C74) suggests sequential roles, with Rab11-dependent RE trafficking preceding Rab8-dependent post-Golgi trafficking. The lack of Rab5 effect (C75) appropriately rules out early endosome involvement. However, the incomplete block by Rab11DN suggests additional trafficking routes exist.

result: GluA1 can traffic from dendritic ERGIC to REs and reach the plasma membrane even when the somatic Golgi is disrupted by BFA treatment. While BFA reduces surface delivery to 25.3% of control levels, this still represents 2.4-fold over background, indicating substantial GA-independent trafficking.
evaluation: Claims C76-C83, C113, C115-C116 demonstrate GA-independent trafficking using BFA. The experimental design appropriately uses temperature block to accumulate cargo in ERGIC before BFA treatment, circumventing BFA's ER export block. The rapid GA dispersal (C76) contrasts with intact ERGIC/REs (C77), validating the approach. The continued co-trafficking with REs (C78, C80) and partial surface delivery (C79, C82) despite GA disruption provide strong evidence. The reduction but not elimination of delivery (C82) is appropriately interpreted as mixed GA-dependent and GA-independent routes.

result: Unlike GluA1, both NL1 and VSV-G surface expression is completely blocked by BFA, indicating that not all secretory cargoes follow the GA-independent trafficking route and that trafficking itineraries diverge after ERGIC accumulation.
evaluation: Claims C84 and C101 demonstrate cargo-specific trafficking routes. The complete BFA sensitivity of NL1 and VSV-G (C84) contrasts with partial GluA1 resistance, indicating cargo-selective mechanisms. This is important for establishing that GA-bypass is not universal but cargo-specific. The inference that itineraries diverge post-ERGIC (C101) is logical given all cargoes initially accumulate in ERGIC but show differential BFA sensitivity.

result: Dendritically photoconverted mEOS-GluA1 colocalizes with TfR-labeled REs in the same dendritic branches with minimal accumulation in somatic GA, demonstrating that dendritic secretory cargo remains spatially constrained throughout the ER→ERGIC→RE pathway.
evaluation: Claims C85-C87 combine photoconversion with RE tracking to demonstrate end-to-end spatial segregation. The colocalization with REs in photoconverted branches (C85) with minimal somatic GA accumulation (C86) extends the spatial segregation findings to the RE stage. This provides strong evidence that local trafficking is maintained throughout the entire dendritic secretory pathway, not just at the ER-ERGIC transition.

result: The majority (88%) of surface GluA1 and a significant fraction (40%) of surface GluA2 are sensitive to endoH, indicating they retain immature glycosylation consistent with GA bypass. In contrast, TARPγ8 is completely endoH resistant, supporting cargo-specific trafficking routes.
evaluation: Claims C88-C90 and C117 provide biochemical evidence for GA-bypass using endoH sensitivity as a marker of immature glycosylation. The high endoH sensitivity of endogenous surface GluA1/A2 (C88, C89) supports physiological relevance beyond the FM-tagged constructs. The complete endoH resistance of TARPγ8 (C90) in the same preparation provides an internal control and supports cargo-specific routing. The data are consistent with prior work (Hanus et al., 2016) and strengthen the GA-bypass model.

result: Background claims establishing that dendrites support local translation, contain mRNAs for secretory proteins, have contiguous ER but lack Golgi apparatus in ~80% of dendrites, and that cargo exiting dendritic ER is directed to ERGICs.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C10-C19, C95-C97 represent established background knowledge appropriately cited from the literature. These claims provide necessary context for the study's motivation and are well-supported by the cited references. They establish the fundamental problem: how do dendrites handle secretory trafficking without Golgi?

result: Background claims about ERGIC-RE interactions, RE involvement in anterograde trafficking in other cell types, RE distribution in dendrites and spines, and examples of GA-independent trafficking for specific cargoes like CFTR.
evaluation: Claims C20-C24, C105-C110, and C112 represent relevant background from the literature that motivates the hypothesis of RE involvement in dendritic forward trafficking. These are appropriately cited and provide context for why REs are candidate organelles for GA-bypass trafficking. The claims about ERGIC-RE interactions (C20, C21) and RE roles in other systems (C22, C23, C106) provide precedent for the proposed mechanism.

result: Background claims about VSV-G trafficking in dendrites from prior studies, showing both somatic GA-directed and locally trapped ERGIC populations, and that GluA1 and NL1 follow the same initial itinerary as VSV-G.
evaluation: Claims C98-C100 appropriately cite prior work on VSV-G trafficking and extend it to show that synaptic proteins follow similar initial routes. The observation that GluA1/NL1 follow the same initial itinerary as VSV-G (C100) is supported by the ERGIC colocalization data, though the inference could be strengthened with direct VSV-G comparison experiments in the same system.

result: Summary claims stating the main conclusions: synaptic proteins undergo spatially restricted trafficking to dendritic ERGICs, then to REs which are critical for PM delivery, and this can occur even when GA is disrupted, representing a GA-independent trafficking network.
evaluation: Claims C91, C93, and C94 represent high-level summary conclusions that are well-supported by the collective experimental evidence from multiple complementary approaches (photoconversion, colocalization, co-trafficking, dominant-negative Rabs, BFA treatment, and endoH sensitivity). These conclusions appropriately integrate the findings into a coherent model.

result: Speculative claim that local secretory processing in dendrites may yield an exclusive repertoire of posttranslational modifications that could uniquely impact protein structure and function.
evaluation: Claim C118 is explicitly speculative and represents a hypothesis for future investigation rather than a demonstrated result. While the endoH sensitivity data support immature glycosylation, the functional consequences and full repertoire of modifications remain unexplored. This is appropriately presented as speculation in the discussion.
